faq.q: Can you really hear the sea in a shell?
faq.a: No. What you hear is the quiet noise around you, boosted by the air inside the shell resonating. It sounds like waves, but it would sound the same in a desert.
asks: Is the sea trapped in a shell?
Why does a shell sound like waves?

faq.a: Resonance is when something vibrates strongly because it is pushed at its own natural rate. The air in a shell has natural pitches, and it boosts any sounds that match them.
asks: How does resonance make sound louder?

faq.q: Is the sound in a shell my blood?
faq.a: Mostly not. Your blood flow makes a little sound, but the main whoosh comes from room noise resonating in the shell. In a soundproof room, the shell goes almost silent.
asks: Do I hear my heartbeat in a shell?
Is the shell sound my pulse?

faq.q: Why do different shells sound different?
faq.a: Each shell has a different shape and size of air space inside, so it resonates at different pitches. Bigger shells boost lower sounds and give a deeper rumble.
asks: Why do big shells sound deeper?
Do all shells make the same sound?

faq.q: Can other things sound like the sea?
faq.a: Yes. Cupping your hand over your ear or holding a mug or glass to it also makes a sea-like sound, because the air inside resonates in the same way.
asks: Why does a cup to my ear sound like the ocean?
Can I hear the sea in a glass?

facts: The sea sound in a shell is ambient noise amplified by resonance in the shell's air cavity.
A larger shell has a larger air cavity and resonates at lower pitches.
